content: Pronation refers to a specific type of rotational movement that can occur in both the forearm and the foot. In the forearm, this movement takes place at the radioulnar joint, while in the foot, it occurs at the subtalar and talocalcaneonavicular joints. In the forearm, pronation involves rotating the palm of the hand from an anterior-facing position (facing forward in the anatomical position) to a posterior-facing position (facing backward). Importantly, this movement does not involve the shoulder joint (glenohumeral joint). The muscles responsible for this action are the pronator quadratus and pronator teres. It is crucial to distinguish pronation of the forearm from medial rotation of the shoulder. Medial rotation of the shoulder can contribute to a similar change in the palm's orientation, but it is a separate movement. To isolate forearm pronation, one can position the elbows against the trunk, flexed at 90 degrees, with the forearms pointing forward and the palms facing upward. From this position, rotating the forearms so that the palms face downward constitutes pronation of the forearm. In the foot, pronation describes a movement where the sole of the foot faces more laterally compared to its position in the anatomical stance. A pronated foot is characterized by the inward angling of the heel bone and a tendency for the arch to collapse. This is often observed in individuals with a knock-kneed posture, where the feet are excessively pronated. During walking or running, pronation allows the foot to absorb shock as the heel strikes the ground and aids in maintaining balance during the mid-stance phase of the gait cycle. However, excessive or habitual pronation can lead to various musculoskeletal issues, including foot pain, knee pain, shin splints, Achilles tendinitis, and plantar fasciitis.
